profile.reading:
Per Flexential's own individual facility page, this building (Flexential Atlanta - Douglasville 2) is located at 1750 N. River Road, Douglasville, GA 30122. The operator publishes a footprint of 358,000 square feet and 36 MW of critical load UPS capacity for this specific building, with published certifications and compliance attestations including HITRUST CSF, PCI DSS, SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, NIST 800-53, ITAR, SSAE 18. Georgia is projected to waive about $296 million in sales and use taxes for data center equipment this year under two statewide exemption programs, one for large or hyperscale projects (adopted around 2018, modeled on a similar Virginia law) and one for bulk computer equipment purchases; the state has waived at least $163 million annually since 2022, with waivers projected to exceed $327 million by 2026, according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution's reporting on state tax-expenditure audits. A 2022 University of Georgia audit found the hyperscale program alone cost the state $5 million in 2018, rising to a projected $57 million by 2030. Georgia is one of 10 states projected to waive nine-figure sums annually through these programs, and in 2024 the state legislature passed a bill to suspend the hyperscale exemption for review, which Governor Brian Kemp vetoed, citing concerns about undermining investment. Metro Atlanta's data center corridor spans several submarkets, including the Douglasville area west of the city (home to Flexential's two largest local buildings), and the Alpharetta/Norcross corridor in the northern suburbs.

Georgia Power's own capacity forecasts illustrate how fast data center demand has grown in the state: the utility projected needing just 400 megawatts of new capacity over seven years in 2022, a figure that jumped to 6,600 megawatts in 2023 and reached 8,500 megawatts by 2025 as data centers proliferated, according to Atlanta Tech News' reporting. In December 2025 Georgia's Public Service Commission approved 9,985 megawatts of new generation, with about 80% of it expected to serve data center demand specifically. The Commission has said data center revenue should reduce rather than increase residential electricity bills, and cited protections including quarterly reporting on new data center activity, longer contract terms with minimum billing so data centers pay for infrastructure even if they relocate, and a Georgia Power financial backstop through 2031 if expected contracts fail to materialize; critics have argued these safeguards remain insufficient and pushed for stronger disclosure and revised tax-incentive terms reflecting current market conditions rather than 2018-era assumptions.

profile.regional_context: Metro Atlanta is one of the largest US data center markets, sustained in part by Georgia's sales-tax exemptions for large data center equipment purchases, a policy that has drawn scrutiny over hundreds of millions of dollars in annual forgone state tax revenue even as it continues to attract large operators to submarkets including Douglasville, Alpharetta, and Norcross.

reading.body:
Flexential Atlanta—Douglasville 2 publishes 36 MW of IT capacity, the largest declared single facility footprint in Georgia, and alone represents 86 percent of the state's published megawatt capacity among mapped data centers.

The 358,000 square feet of technical space can support between 900 and 3,600 racks depending on workload density. At 40 kW per rack, a density associated with AI training, the facility holds roughly 900 racks. At 10 kW per rack, typical for colocation, it scales to 3,600. The operator has not disclosed which density applies, so actual rack count remains an assumption tied to tenant workload mix.

The certification stack—HITRUST CSF, PCI DSS, SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, NIST 800-53, ITAR, and SSAE 18—qualifies the facility to host regulated workloads in finance, healthcare, payments, and defense applications. ITAR clearance in particular narrows the field of eligible operators and admits tenants handling controlled technical data for defense purposes. No certification directly enables or restricts AI compute.

Georgia has 33 mapped facilities on this site. Only two publish a megawatt figure. This published scarcity reflects the difficulty of extracting capacity data from operator websites rather than true distribution, meaning the real concentration of Georgia capacity across available facilities remains unknown.
